extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism and public opinion; newspaper editors and media critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria governing what newspapers publish and why: the economic incentives (advertisers, circulation), reader loyalty and habits, editorial strategies to retain audiences, and the epistemic/formal conditions that make an occurrence 'news'. Useful for analyzing or teaching news selection and press behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation as means to an end
rubrics_metrics.description: "Circulation is, therefore, the means to an end."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation is not an end in itself but the mechanism by which a paper achieves economic goals (chiefly advertising revenue). The passage explains that the paper pursues the kind of circulation an advertiser will buy; types of circulation ("quality" or "mass") are valued differently depending on what advertisers want. Example/implication: editors must aim for the audience profile advertisers value rather than merely maximizing raw numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers determine valuable circulation (quality vs mass)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers buy space in those publications "which are fairly certain to reach their future customers." The kind of circulation the advertiser will buy depends on what he has to sell — it may be "quality" or "mass."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers should evaluate circulation by its attractiveness to likely advertisers: reaching fairly prosperous households is often most valuable. Editorial and marketing decisions (content, geographic reach) should be informed by what customers advertisers seek. Anti-pattern: pursuing circulation among groups with low advertising value (e.g., exclusively the very poor) unless advertiser demand justifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not alienate the buying public
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper which angers those whom it pays is a bad medium for an advertiser. If it alienates the buying public, it loses the best asset of its existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must balance investigative or adversarial journalism with the need to retain readers who constitute the buying public. Alienating the core audience risks losing advertising revenue and circulation loyalty. The quote implies publishers may compromise (or appear to) to avoid losing readers' support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect payment expectations (news as quasi-gratis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The information must come naturally; that is to say gratis, if not out of the heart of the 'citizen, then gratis out of the newspaper. The citizen will pay for his telephone... but will pay handsomely for the privilege of having someone read about him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect news as part of an invisible environment paid for indirectly (through advertisers) rather than as a direct priced good. This expectation shapes pricing models (free/low-cost papers supported by ads) and editorial choices toward content readers feel entitled to receive without explicit payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central/metropolitan papers supply general news
rubrics_metrics.description: These 'key papers' collect news dealing with great events and make up the great press associations which cooperate in the exchange of news; the whole press of the nation may depend on reports of a few metropolitan dailies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the hierarchical structure of news flow: local/rural papers often rely on metropolitan services for general and international news. This influences resource allocation, editorial focus, and the comparative value of investigative vs. routine reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty is informal and habit-based
rubrics_metrics.description: The loyalty of the buying public to a newspaper is not stipulated in any bond... The reader is the sole and the daily judge of his loyalty, and there can be no suit against him for breach of promise or nonsupport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retention strategies must cultivate habits and obscure elements of attachment (local coverage, personal mentions, ritual features). There is no legal or contractual guarantee of loyalty; editors must sustain it through content and routine rather than subscriptions alone (in metropolitan dailies subscriptions are not the primary bond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers judge primarily by personal relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most men tend to hold the newspaper most strictly accountable in their capacity, not of general readers, but of special pleaders on matters of their own experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability and perceived accuracy are strongest on topics tied to readers' lived experience (local facts, business, church/school items). Editorials and reporting should ensure correctness and sensitivity in those domains to maintain credibility and loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes and confirmation shape reader reception
rubrics_metrics.description: They do not boggle over such news if it conforms to their stereotypes, and they continue to read it if it interests them. The canon of truth cannot be applied. They are dealing here with a subject matter which ... is indistinguishable from fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers often accept items that fit preconceptions even if not rigorously true; papers may exploit this tendency. For rigorous public information, editors must be aware of stereotype-confirming bias and the risk of publishing items that read like fiction for some audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: The nature of news: requires an unmistakable manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Something definite must occur that has unmistakable form — it may be an arrest, a denunciation, a riot, a sale, a wage-schedule, a price change, the proposal to build a bridge. There must be a manifestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic newsworthiness is tied to concrete, objectified acts or events that can be named and pinned down. Reporters should seek manifestations with clear form to avoid relying on rumor or speculation; legal and ethical constraints (libel) require anchoring stories in observable acts or public records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record-keeping machinery yields precise news
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever there is a good machinery of record, the modern news service works with great precision ... There is one on the stock exchange ... there is a machinery for election returns ... deaths, births, marriages and divorces are recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics with reliable recording systems (financial markets, election tallies, vital records, customs) support precise, dependable reporting. News organizations should leverage official records and institutional reporting systems to increase accuracy and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics lacking objective records are debatable or neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: All news about states of mind ... policies of foreign governments ... private profit ... wages ... involve data that are at best spasmodically recorded. Then the news on these subjects is bound to be debatable, when it is not wholly neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When objective measurement or documentation is absent, reporting will be contestable and prone to opinion, inference, or neglect. Editors must treat such topics with methodological care (investigation, sourcing, caveats) and recognize limitations in claiming definitive knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/community diary function as retention strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of becoming ... the printed diary of the home town is one that every newspaper ... must in some measure fill ... publish local items: weddings, funerals, lodge meetings, school prizes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including localized, personal-interest content (society items, local events) is a deliberate editorial strategy to create attachment and dependable circulation. Papers should balance broader reporting with community notices to build a devoted reader base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial mix: entertainments and special pages to attract readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many papers go to the dazzling levels of society, to sports, pictures, actresses, advice to the lovelorn, high-school notes, women's pages, buyer's pages, cooking receipts, chess, whist, gardening, comic strips ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure steady circulation beyond general news, newspapers deploy a variety of sections and features targeting interests (sports, society, advice, women's pages, comics). Editorial planning should consider which features reliably drive habitual readership for their market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic structure shapes professional standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The salaries of newspaper men ... reporting is the least regarded ... The rewards in journalism go to specialty work ... executives, and to men with a knack and flavor of their own ... The able men take up straight reporting with the intention of leaving as soon as possible ... this is the chief reason why it has never developed ... corporate traditions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The market value of different journalistic roles affects recruitment, retention, and professionalization. Weak remuneration and career incentives for routine reporting undermine the development of stable professional standards. Organizational leaders should consider pay structures and career paths to strengthen reporting craft and institutional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal constraint: avoid publishing unverified rumors (libel risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apart from the fact that none of this could be published because it would be libel, there is in these rumors nothing definite on which to peg a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must avoid publishing unverified allegations about private individuals; stories need definite facts or public records. Legal risk and ethical standards require reliance on verifiable manifestations rather than gossip or anonymous rumor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence increases with diversified advertiser base
rubrics_metrics.description: It may seem like a contradiction (yet it is the truth) to assert: the greater the number of advertisers, the less dependence on the advertiser!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A diversified advertising base reduces dependence on any single advertiser's influence, potentially increasing editorial independence. Editors and publishers should consider revenue diversification as a structural safeguard for editorial autonomy.
